kurz: Tax on trading gains is calculated per calendar year, regardless of how a strategy develops, and almost none of a trader's trading expenses are deductible.

bloecke.md:
Every closed position is a taxable event. It makes no difference whether it belonged to a series that only pays off over two years or whether its gain was already earmarked for the next trade. The tax is calculated per calendar year. The results are allocated to loss pots that the trader cannot choose, and the tax is deducted at source before the money can be deployed again.

This gives rise to three effects through which a strategy that works on paper can fail in the portfolio. The tax falls due early, it is levied on gross results, and the costs of running the trading operation are not taken into account. Together with fees and the spread, these effects considerably raise the threshold above which trading pays off.

## Tax rate and type of income

Private trading gives rise to income from capital assets and not to business income. A separate tax rate of 25% applies under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act), plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge, making 26.375% in total. With church tax, it is 27.82% (8%, Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg) or 27.995% (9%). This rate applies regardless of whether ten or ten thousand orders were placed in the year.

The provision under which a transaction falls does not change the tax rate. It does, however, determine which loss pot a loss ends up in. Of all the tax distinctions, this one has the greatest financial consequences in trading.

bloecke.md:
There are two loss pots, and offsetting only works in one direction. Losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from the sale of shares (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG). All other losses sit in the general pot and may also reduce share gains, but not the other way round. Trading individual shares and derivatives in parallel therefore creates two separate calculations that, in the worst case, do not offset each other.

For derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte), there used to be a cap on loss offsetting, most recently €20,000 a year. The Annual Tax Act 2024 of 2 December 2024 abolished it without replacement, applicable in all open cases. Guides, forum posts and tax calculators that still work with this limit are out of date. For CFD, futures and options traders, this was the most important change of recent years.

bloecke.titel: Loss after the turn of the year
bloecke.md:
An account closes December with a realised net gain of €40,000. The bank has withheld around €10,550 of this at 26.375%, assuming that the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) has already been used up. In January, the same strategy loses the same €40,000.

Economically, the trader is back at zero before tax. The tax paid in the previous year is nevertheless final. The January loss forms a new loss pot that only takes effect against future gains. It can be carried forward indefinitely but cannot be carried back to the previous year (Section 20(6) sentences 1 to 3 EStG). In addition, the trading capital is permanently €10,550 smaller, and with it every future position.

bloecke.titel: Trading year with €50,000 of capital, from gross to net
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with 100 round turns a year at full account size, total costs of 0.10% per round turn and a saver's allowance of €1,000 that has not yet been used. A gross 16% becomes a net 4.9%.

bloecke.md:
The saver's allowance of €1,000 (€2,000 for joint assessment, Section 20(9) EStG) lowers the tax burden in this example from 26.375% to 17.6% of the result before tax. This is the only respect in which a small trading account is better off for tax purposes than a large one. However, the allowance applies only once per year and person.

The calculation can also be reversed. It then shows how much a strategy has to earn gross for a modest net return to remain after costs and tax. The result depends almost entirely on the trading frequency. Costs grow linearly with the number of round turns, whereas the tax only covers what is left after costs.

bloecke.titel: Gross return required for a net 4%
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with total costs of 0.10% per round turn (fee, half the spread per side, slippage) on the full account volume, followed by 26.375% tax on the result after costs, without the saver's allowance.

bloecke.md: With 250 round turns, the strategy has to earn more than 30% a year for 4% to remain. Mistakes, slippage outliers and losing streaks are not yet included. Tax planning does not change this. The most important lever is the trading frequency; the tax acts only as a factor on the result after costs.

bloecke.md:
## Liquidity and timing of the tax

The custodian bank offsets gains and losses on an ongoing basis within a year. If a later loss enters the pot, it refunds tax already withheld (Section 43a(3) EStG). It does not do this across the turn of the year. Investors who trade with several brokers also have to bring gains and losses together themselves. For this, they need a loss certificate (Verlustbescheinigung) under Section 43a(3) sentence 4 EStG. The application must reach the bank by 15 December and is irrevocable (Section 43a(3) sentence 5 EStG).

A second need for liquidity arises in January. For fund units in the portfolio, the bank automatically debits the tax on the [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum]] from the settlement account. The base interest rate (Basiszins) for 2026 is 3.20% (BMF circular of 13 January 2026), the highest value since the advance lump sum was introduced. The base return (Basisertrag) is therefore 2.24% of the value at the start of the year. The advance lump sum for 2026 is deemed to have been received on the first working day of 2027. If all of an account's capital is tied up in positions, there is no balance available for this debit. The result is debit interest if the bank collects the amount via an arranged overdraft, or a report to the tax office, which then claims the tax (Section 44(1) EStG).

bloecke.titel: Worked example of the advance lump sum
bloecke.md:
On 1 January 2026, €50,000 is invested in an equity ETF. The increase in value over the year is well above the advance lump sum.

- The base return is €50,000 × 3.20% × 0.7 = €1,120.
- After deducting the 30% [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption]] (Section 20 InvStG), €784 remains.
- The tax on this is €784 × 26.375% = €206.78.

If the saver's allowance has not yet been used up, no tax is due. The advance lump sum is no argument against a savings plan. It is, however, a reason to have a balance on the settlement account in January.

## Option writer's premiums

Premiums from writing options are taxable in full when received (Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG). If the option writer later buys the option back, the premiums paid for this reduce the income, but only in the year of closing out. If the premium is collected in December and the option is bought back in January, the option writer pays tax in the first year on a premium that, economically, they never earned. The deduction only takes effect in the second year.

If instead the option writer is called upon to pay a cash settlement, this payment counts for tax purposes as a loss from a [[Derivative transaction (Termingeschäft)|derivative transaction]] and does not reduce the premium income. Since the €20,000 limit was abolished, such a loss can be offset without any limit on the amount.

## Records and foreign brokers

With a German custodian bank, the tax is settled by the deduction of the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer). What is then needed is the annual tax certificate and, with several securities accounts, the loss certificate applied for in good time. Foreign brokers, which are the rule rather than the exception in futures and options trading, do not deduct any capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer). Income from such accounts must always be declared in the tax return (Section 32d(3) EStG). The calculation, the conversion of foreign currency amounts into euros and the allocation to the pots are the investor's own responsibility.

Active traders should therefore keep three types of records: the broker's complete annual statements, the acquisition data of transferred positions and the evidence relating to foreign currency balances. If the acquisition data are missing after a securities account transfer, the bank applies a flat 30% of the sale proceeds as the tax base (Section 43a(2) EStG), regardless of the actual gain. In the view of the tax authorities, switching foreign currency balances does not fall under the flat-rate withholding tax. Under Section 23 EStG, it counts as a private disposal transaction (privates Veräußerungsgeschäft) with a one-year period and a €1,000 exemption threshold (Freigrenze). A trading journal, which should be kept anyway, in practice also covers these obligations.

bloecke.titel: Realised gains and losses over the full year and in December
bloecke.unter: Odean (1998), around 10,000 US brokerage accounts, 1987-1993. PGR and PLR measure the proportion of realised gain and loss positions respectively, relative to the gain and loss positions that could have been realised.

bloecke.md: In December the ratio reverses, that is, at the time when selling at a loss brings a tax advantage. This shows that investors are able to realise losses. In the other eleven months, they sell losing positions much less often than winning positions. For traders, a year-end review is therefore justified. At the same time, it is the point at which tax reasons begin to determine trading decisions. A position that should be held under your own rules should not be sold solely because the sale fills a loss pot.

1. If there are gains at one broker and losses at another, apply for the loss certificate. The application must reach the bank by 15 December and is irrevocable.
2. Check whether the saver's allowance has been used up and whether the exemption orders (Freistellungsaufträge) are correctly distributed.
3. Check whether there is enough balance on the settlement account for the advance lump sum in January.
4. For foreign brokers, check whether all annual statements are available and the amounts have been converted into euros.

Closing positions purely for tax reasons does not belong on this list.

Frequent trading almost never turns the income into business income. According to the established case law of the Federal Fiscal Court (BFH), buying and selling securities in your own name and for your own account remains private asset management (private Vermögensverwaltung), even with high volumes, short holding periods and debt financing. Classification as a business requires acting for the account of others or appearing in the market in a manner typical of a dealer.

This classification has advantages and disadvantages. Commercial traders may deduct monitors, data feeds and seminars and offset losses against other income, although losses from derivative transactions can in principle only be offset against gains from derivative transactions (Section 15(4) sentence 3 EStG). Private investors may do neither, but in return they pay the flat rate of 25% instead of their personal tax rate.

mitnehmen: Because the calendar year is the tax period, gains in December are not offset against losses in January, and the tax paid permanently reduces the trading capital.
Share losses may only be offset against gains from share sales; all other losses sit in the general pot. The €20,000 limit for derivative transactions was abolished by the Annual Tax Act 2024.
Almost none of the costs of running a trading operation are tax-deductible. Order fees reduce the gain; data feeds, software and seminars do not (Section 20(9) EStG).
To make 4% after costs and tax, a gross return of just over 15% is needed with 100 round turns a year, and more than 30% with 250 round turns.
For liquidity planning, allow for the ongoing tax deduction during the year, the 15 December deadline for the loss certificate and the debit for the advance lump sum in January.

Payment for granting an option. It is taxable in full in the year it is received (Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG). Premiums paid for a closing transaction reduce the income only in the year of closing out.
